# Comparing versions of files {#sec-git-diff}

Git allows us to compare different versions of files, whether they are in the working tree, the staging area, or different commits. In this chapter, we will learn how to use the `git diff` command to make these comparisons and how to interpret the differences it displays.


## Compare the working tree and the staging area

Using `git diff` with no arguments will show changes in the working tree that are not in the staging area. This allows us to inspect changes to tracked files before adding them to the staging area using `git add .`.

Let's illustrate this with an example. First, we initialize a new Git repository and create a file in the working tree:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/example01-git-diff
$ cd ~/example01-git-diff
$ git init
$ echo "Contents of file1.txt" > file1.txt
</pre>

Now let's run `git diff`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff

</pre>

Notice that `git diff` produces no output. This is because `file1.txt` is an untracked file at this point, and the staging area is empty, so there is nothing for `git diff` to compare. Let's add `file1.txt` to the staging area and commit the file, then make additional changes in the working tree and run `git diff` again:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Add file1.txt"
$ echo "New content in working tree" >> file1.txt
$ git diff
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 85e8799..ebfc449 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1 +1,2 @@</span>
 Contents of file1.txt
<span class="col-diff-addition">+New content in working tree</span>

</pre>

`git diff` now shows us the changes in the working tree relative to the staging area. In this example, it shows that we have added the line "New content in the working tree" to `file1.txt`.


## Understanding the diff output

As you saw in the example in the previous section, the output from `git diff` contains several elements worth explaining. We will use the preceding example to explain the different parts of the output.


### Structure of `git diff` output

For each file being compared, Git displays a separate section of the diff output, beginning with a *file header* that identifies the file. Within each file section, Git groups changes into one or more *hunks*, which are sections of the file containing changes and surrounding unchanged lines. Each hunk begins with a *hunk header*.

In our simple example, only one file has been modified, and its changes are contained in a single hunk.


### The file header

The first line of each file section is called the file header:

<pre class="terminal">
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
</pre>

The file header identifies the two versions of the file being compared. Git uses the prefixes `a/` and `b/` to distinguish them. These prefixes do not indicate actual directories, but represent the original and modified versions of the file, respectively.

In our example, where we use `git diff` without arguments, `a/file1.txt` refers to the version in the staging area, while `b/file1.txt` refers to the version in the working tree.

The prefix `diff --git` might suggest that Git has executed the Bash command `diff` with a `--git` option, but this is not the case. Instead, `diff --git` is part of the output format generated by Git.


### File metadata

The second line

<pre class="terminal">
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 85e8799..ebfc449 100644</span>
</pre>

displays some Git metadata. We will not examine this metadata in detail, but simply note that `85e8799` and `ebfc449` are abbreviated object IDs identifying the two versions of the file being compared. In addition to the `index` line, Git may display other metadata, such as `new file mode 100644` when a file has been added or `deleted file mode 100644` when a file has been deleted.


### Markers for changes

The next two lines establish which symbols are associated with each version of the file:

<pre class="terminal">
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
</pre>

The `---` line associates the `-` symbol with the original version of the file (`a/file1.txt`), while the `+++` line associates the `+` symbol with the modified version (`b/file1.txt`). These symbols are used in the diff content to indicate which lines are present in one version but not the other.


### The hunk header

The next line

<pre class="terminal">
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1 +1,2 @@</span>
</pre>

is called the hunk header. It identifies the line ranges shown in the hunk for each of the two versions being compared.

The part beginning with `-` refers to the original version of the file, while the part beginning with `+` refers to the modified version as established by the markers explained above. Each part contains the starting line number followed by the number of lines shown, separated by a comma.

In our example, `-1` indicates that the hunk contains one line from the original version, starting at line `1`. Similarly, `+1,2` indicates that the hunk contains two lines from the modified version, starting at line `1`.

When only one line is shown, the number of lines is omitted, as in `-1`.

A file may contain multiple hunks, each with its own hunk header. We will see an example of this later in the chapter.


### The diff content

The remaining output

<pre class="terminal">
 Contents of file1.txt
<span class="col-diff-addition">+New content in working tree</span>
</pre>

contains the *diff content*, which consists of individual *diff lines* that can be divided into three types:

- Context lines: Lines that have not changed between the two versions. These lines help you understand where in the file changes are happening. By default, these lines are shown in grey. In our example, the `Contents of file1.txt` line is a context line, since it is present in both versions of the file. These lines are preceded by a space rather than a `+` or `-`.

- Deletion lines: Lines that were present in the original version, but are not present in the modified version. These lines are preceded by a `-`. By default, these lines are shown in red. Our current example does not contain any deletion lines.

- Addition lines: Lines that are present in the modified version, but were not present in the original version. These lines are preceded by a `+`. By default, these lines are shown in green. In our example, `New content in working tree` is an addition line.

Together, these lines show how the file differs between two versions. When an existing line is modified, Git typically represents the change as a deletion of the original line followed by an addition of the modified line. The surrounding context lines help us understand where the changes occur in the file.


### General structure of diff output

The following schematic summarizes how Git organizes diff output into file sections and hunks. When differences are found, the output consists of one or more file sections, each beginning with a file header and associated metadata. Within each file section, changes are grouped into one or more hunks, each beginning with a hunk header followed by the lines showing the changes. The number of file sections and hunks depends on the files being compared and the changes made to them.

```{=html}
<div class="diff-structure">

  <!-- First file section -->
  <div class="diff-file">
    <div class="diff-file-title">
      File section 1
    </div>

    <div class="diff-file-content">

      <div class="diff-component">
        <div class="diff-component-title">
          File header and metadata
        </div>
        <div class="diff-component-description">
          diff --git, index, ---, +++
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="diff-component">
        <div class="diff-component-title">Hunk 1</div>
        <div class="diff-component-description">
          @@ ... @@ followed by diff lines
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="diff-ellipsis">...</div>

      <div class="diff-component">
        <div class="diff-component-title">Hunk m</div>
        <div class="diff-component-description">
          @@ ... @@ followed by diff lines
        </div>
      </div>

    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- Additional file sections -->
  <div class="diff-ellipsis">...</div>

  <!-- Last file section -->
  <div class="diff-file">
    <div class="diff-file-title">
      File section n
    </div>

    <div class="diff-file-content">

      <div class="diff-component">
        <div class="diff-component-title">
          File header and metadata
        </div>
        <div class="diff-component-description">
          diff --git, index, ---, +++
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="diff-component">
        <div class="diff-component-title">Hunk 1</div>
        <div class="diff-component-description">
          @@ ... @@ followed by diff lines
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="diff-ellipsis">...</div>

      <div class="diff-component">
        <div class="diff-component-title">Hunk m</div>
        <div class="diff-component-description">
          @@ ... @@ followed by diff lines
        </div>
      </div>

    </div>
  </div>

</div>
```


## Understanding diff output with changes to multiple files

Now that we can interpret the output of `git diff`, let's look at a slightly more realistic example of a diff with changes to multiple files. First, we create a repository containing two files, commit them, and then modify both files:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/example02-git-diff
$ cd ~/example02-git-diff
$ git init
$ touch file1.txt
$ touch file2.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Add file1.txt and file2.txt"
$ echo "Contents of file1.txt" >> file1.txt
$ echo "Contents of file2.txt" >> file2.txt
</pre>

Next, we run `git diff`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index e69de29..85e8799 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -0,0 +1 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Contents of file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file2.txt b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index e69de29..92e49c3 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -0,0 +1 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Contents of file2.txt</span>

</pre>

Notice that the output contains two separate file sections, one for `file1.txt` and another for `file2.txt`. Each section begins with a file header (`diff --git`) identifying the file being compared, followed by metadata and the changes to that file. In this example, each file section contains a single hunk, identified by its hunk header (`@@ ... @@`).


## Understanding diff output with multiple changes to a file

When a file contains multiple changes, and these changes are not near each other, Git may divide the changes into multiple hunks rather than displaying the entire file, with a few context lines around each change. Let's illustrate this using the Bash command `seq` to create a file with 20 numbered lines. We then use `sed` to modify its first and last lines of the file. You do not need to understand the syntax of these commands; they are used only to prepare the example.

First, we create a repository where we create and commit the file, then modify its first and last lines:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/example03-git-diff
$ cd ~/example03-git-diff
$ git init
$ seq 1 20 > file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Add file1.txt"
$ sed -i '1s/.*/Modified first line/' file1.txt
$ sed -i '$s/.*/Modified last line/' file1.txt
</pre>

Next, we execute `git diff`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 0ff3bbb..b5ad34d 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-deletion">-1</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Modified first line</span>
 2
 3
 4
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -17,4 +17,4 @@</span>
 17
 18
 19
<span class="col-diff-deletion">-20</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Modified last line</span>

</pre>

Notice that the diff contains two hunks because the changes occur in different parts of the file. Each hunk has its own hunk header, indicating which lines from the original and modified versions are shown. The first hunk shows a change to line 1, while the second shows a change to line 20. Each hunk also contains a few surrounding context lines.


## Compare the staging area with the current commit

To compare the staging area with the current commit (`HEAD`), we can use `git diff --staged`. This will show us the changes that have been added using `git add` and would be included in the next commit if `git commit` were executed. When the repository has no commits, Git compares the staging area with an empty version of the repository containing no files.

In Git, `HEAD` is a special reference that identifies the current commit. We can use `HEAD` to refer to this commit without having to specify its commit ID. Git references, including `HEAD`, are explained in more detail in @sec-git-references.

Let's illustrate this with a new example. First, we create a repository and stage a new file:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/example04-git-diff
$ cd ~/example04-git-diff
$ git init
$ echo "Original content" > file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
</pre>

We can now execute `git diff --staged` to see the changes we have staged:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff --staged
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">new file mode 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 0000000..3b94cd9</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- /dev/null</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -0,0 +1 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Original content</span>
</pre>

Notice the `/dev/null` output in the markers. The marker `--- /dev/null` indicates that the file does not exist in the original version being compared.

Next, we commit the staged changes, modify the file, stage the modification, and run `git diff --staged` again:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git commit -m "Add file1.txt"
$ echo "Change original content" > file1.txt
$ git add .
$ git diff --staged
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 3b94cd9..74e17e4 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1 +1 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-deletion">-Original content</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Change original content</span>
</pre>

Notice that Git represents the modified line as a deletion of the original line followed by an addition of the new line. The original line `Original content` is present in `HEAD` but has been replaced in the staging area.


## Compare the working tree with the current commit

Sometimes it is useful to see all differences between the current commit and the working tree, regardless of whether they have been staged or not. To do this we can use `git diff HEAD`, which compares `HEAD` (the current commit) with the working tree. 

Consider the following example, where we first create `file1.txt` containing a single line and commit it. Next, we add another line and stage that change. Finally, we add a third line in the working tree that is not staged:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/example05-git-diff
$ cd ~/example05-git-diff
$ git init
$ echo "Line 1" > file1.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Add file1.txt"
$ echo "Line 2" >> file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ echo "Line 3" >> file1.txt
</pre>

Running `git diff` at this point would show only the unstaged change of adding the third line, and using `git diff --staged` would only show us the staged change of adding the second line. However, running `git diff HEAD` shows both changes:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff HEAD
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 3be9c81..6ad36e5 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1 +1,3 @@</span>
 Line 1
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Line 2</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Line 3</span>
</pre>


## Compare two commits

We can use the form `git diff <commit1> <commit2>` to compare two different commits. 

First, let's create a new repository with three commits:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/example06-git-diff
$ cd ~/example06-git-diff
$ git init
$ echo "Line added in first commit" > file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Add file1.txt"
$ echo "Line added in second commit" >> file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Add line to file1.txt"
$ echo "Completely change contents in third commit" > file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Completely change content of file1.txt"
</pre>

As we have already seen, `HEAD` refers to the current commit. We can also use `HEAD^` to refer to the first parent of the commit identified by `HEAD`. We can therefore use `git diff HEAD^ HEAD` to show the changes introduced in the current commit:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff HEAD^ HEAD
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index cecb547..9dc41f3 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1,2 +1 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-deletion">-Line added in first commit</span>
<span class="col-diff-deletion">-Line added in second commit</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Completely change contents in third commit</span>

</pre>

We can also use `git log --oneline` to find the abbreviated commit IDs of the commits in the repository, then use these to compare the first and third commits:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git log --oneline
<span class="col-hash">1fdab67</span> <span class="col-yellow">(</span><span class="col-head">HEAD</span> <span class="col-yellow">-></span> <span class="col-branch-local">main</span><span class="col-yellow">)</span> Completely change content of file1.txt
<span class="col-hash">d481959</span> Add line to file1.txt
<span class="col-hash">a41cc0a</span> Add file1.txt
$ git diff a41cc0a 1fdab67
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 67b6d9e..9dc41f3 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1 +1 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-deletion">-Line added in first commit</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Completely change contents in third commit</span>

</pre>


## Comparing individual files

By default, `git diff` shows differences for all tracked files that have changed between the versions being compared. However, we can also restrict the comparison to individual files.

For example, to show only unstaged changes to `file1.txt`, we can use:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff -- file1.txt
</pre>

The `--` separates the filename from the other arguments passed to `git diff`. This tells Git that `file1.txt` is a file whose changes we want to inspect.

We can also specify a filename when using other forms of `git diff`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff --staged -- file1.txt
$ git diff HEAD -- file1.txt
$ git diff HEAD^ HEAD -- file1.txt
</pre>

These commands perform the same comparisons introduced earlier in the chapter, but restrict the output to changes involving `file1.txt`.

We can also specify multiple filenames to compare only the selected files:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff -- file1.txt file2.txt
</pre>

## Summary

In this chapter, we have learned how to use `git diff` to compare different states of a Git repository and how to interpret the output it produces. A diff shows the differences between two versions of a file, including added and deleted lines, as well as modified lines represented by deletions and additions. It also shows unchanged lines surrounding the changes to provide context. Understanding this output is useful not only when using `git diff`, but also when using other Git commands that display diffs, such as `git show`.

We have introduced several ways to use `git diff` to compare different states of a repository:

```{=html}
<div style="margin-top:2em; margin-bottom:2em">
<table class="table-striped">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Command</th>
      <th>Comparison</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>  
      <td><code>git diff</code></td>
      <td>Staging area &rarr; Working tree</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code>git diff --staged</code></td>
      <td><code>HEAD</code> &rarr; Staging area</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code>git diff HEAD</code></td>
      <td><code>HEAD</code> &rarr; Working tree</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code>git diff HEAD^ HEAD</code></td>
      <td>Parent of <code>HEAD</code> &rarr; <code>HEAD</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code>git diff &lt;commit1&gt; &lt;commit2&gt;</code></td>
      <td>First commit &rarr; Second commit</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
</div>
```

Remember that the order of the versions being compared matters when using `git diff <commit1> <commit2>`. Changes are presented as additions or deletions relative to the first version, so reversing the order of the versions being compared causes additions to appear as deletions and vice versa.


## Exercises

### Exercise 1 - Interpreting diff output

In this exercise, you will practice interpreting the output of `git diff`. First, create a repository with the following commands:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/ex01-git-diff
$ cd ~/ex01-git-diff
$ git init
$ echo "First line of file1.txt" > file1.txt
$ echo "First line of file2.txt" > file2.txt
</pre>

<b>1. Using `git diff` with untracked files.</b>

Use `git diff` on the current state of the repository. Before running the command, identify the two repository states being compared and predict the output.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

`git diff` shows changes in the working tree that are not in the staging area. Because both `file1.txt` and `file2.txt` are untracked and the staging area is empty, `git diff` will not show any output.

:::

<b>2. Show changes to be committed.</b>

Add `file1.txt` and `file2.txt` to the staging area, and run `git diff --staged` to see the changes that would be committed if `git commit` were run. Before running the command, answer the following questions:

- What states are being compared?

- How many file headers will the diff output contain?

- How many hunks will the diff output contain?

- How many addition and deletion lines will each hunk contain?

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git add file1.txt file2.txt
$ git diff --staged
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">new file mode 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 0000000..edb460f</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- /dev/null</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -0,0 +1 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+First line of file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file2.txt b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">new file mode 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 0000000..2ff87b8</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- /dev/null</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -0,0 +1 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+First line of file2.txt</span>
</pre>

Since the repository does not yet contain any commits, `git diff --staged` compares the staging area with an empty version of the repository containing no files. The output contains two file sections, one for `file1.txt` and another for `file2.txt`. Each file section contains a single hunk with one addition line and no deletion lines, since both files are newly added and contain only one line.

:::

<b>3. Show changes introduced in the current commit.</b>

First, run the following commands to commit the staged changes, then create two additional commits:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git commit -m "Add file1.txt and file2.txt"
$ touch file3.txt
$ git add file3.txt
$ git commit -m "Add file3.txt"
$ echo "Second line in file1.txt" >> file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Add second line to file1.txt"
</pre>

Next, use `git diff HEAD^ HEAD` to show the changes included in the current commit. Before running the command, explain which commits `HEAD^` and `HEAD` identify, and which additions and deletions you expect to see in the diff.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff HEAD^ HEAD
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index edb460f..3366c1d 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1 +1,2 @@</span>
 First line of file1.txt
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Second line in file1.txt</span>
</pre>

`HEAD` refers to the current commit, while `HEAD^` refers to its parent, which is the second commit in this example. The command `git diff HEAD^ HEAD` therefore shows the changes introduced in the third commit. The output contains only one file section, for `file1.txt`, with a single hunk showing one addition line and no deletion lines. This is because the third commit added a line to `file1.txt` without removing or modifying any existing lines.

:::

<b>4. Show changes between two commits.</b>

Use `git log --oneline` to identify the abbreviated commit IDs of the first and third commits in the repository, and then use `git diff <commit1> <commit2>` to show the changes that have been made from the first to the third commit. Before running the command, predict what the diff will show.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git log --oneline
<span class="col-hash">d01e4ee</span> <span class="col-yellow">(</span><span class="col-head">HEAD</span> <span>-></span> <span class="col-branch-local">main</span><span class="col-yellow">)</span> Add second line to file1.txt
<span class="col-hash">81b3aa2</span> Add file3.txt
<span class="col-hash">fa1357c</span> Add file1.txt and file2.txt
$ git diff fa1357c d01e4ee
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index edb460f..3366c1d 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1 +1,2 @@</span>
 First line of file1.txt
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Second line in file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file3.txt b/file3.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">new file mode 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 0000000..e69de29</span>
</pre>

The command compares the first and third commits in the repository. The output contains two file sections, one for `file1.txt` and another for `file3.txt`. The section for `file1.txt` contains a single hunk with one addition line and no deletion lines, since a new line was added to the file between the two commits. The section for `file3.txt` shows that the file was added between the two commits. However, because `file3.txt` is empty, this section contains only a file header and metadata, with no hunks or addition lines. The output does not include `file2.txt` because its contents are identical in both commits.

:::

<pre class="terminal">
$ cd
$ rm -rf ~/ex01-git-diff
</pre>


### Exercise 2 - Practising comparing different states of a repository

In this exercise, you will practice comparing different states of a repository.

First, use the following commands to set up a repository with three empty files that have been added to the staging area:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/ex02-git-diff
$ cd ~/ex02-git-diff
$ git init
$ touch file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt
$ git add .
</pre>

<b>1. Display changes staged for the initial commit.</b>

Use an appropriate invocation of `git diff` to display the changes staged for the initial commit.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff --staged
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">new file mode 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 0000000..e69de29</span>
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file2.txt b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">new file mode 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 0000000..e69de29</span>
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file3.txt b/file3.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">new file mode 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 0000000..e69de29</span>
</pre>

:::

<b>2. Display unstaged changes.</b>

Run the following commands to commit the files, then make changes to `file1.txt` and `file2.txt`, stage some of the changes for `file1.txt`, and stage `file3.txt` for deletion using `git rm`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git commit -m "Add files"
$ echo "Staged contents of file1.txt" >> file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ echo "Unstaged contents of file1.txt" >> file1.txt
$ echo "Unstaged contents of file2.txt" >> file2.txt
$ git rm file3.txt
</pre>

Use an invocation of `git diff` to compare the working tree with the staging area to see which changes remain unstaged.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index c79d91d..caaf2c0 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1 +1,2 @@</span>
 Staged contents of file1.txt
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Unstaged contents of file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file2.txt b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index e69de29..5dd500d 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -0,0 +1 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Unstaged contents of file2.txt</span>
</pre>


:::


<b>3. Compare the working tree with the current commit.</b>

Use an invocation of `git diff` to compare the working tree with the current commit. Before running the command, predict which files will appear in the output. Will the deletion of `file3.txt` be included?

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff HEAD
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index e69de29..caaf2c0 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -0,0 +1,2 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Staged contents of file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Unstaged contents of file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file2.txt b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index e69de29..5dd500d 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -0,0 +1 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Unstaged contents of file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file3.txt b/file3.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">deleted file mode 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index e69de29..0000000</span>
</pre>

The diff contains three file sections, one for each file. For `file1.txt`, both the staged and unstaged changes appear as additions, while `file2.txt` contains only an unstaged addition.

Notice that `file3.txt` also appears in the diff, even though its deletion was already staged using `git rm`. This is because `git diff HEAD` compares the current commit with the working tree, regardless of whether the changes have been staged. Since `file3.txt` existed in the current commit but has been deleted from the working tree, Git displays it as a deleted file.

:::

<b>4. Compare changes to an individual file.</b>

Use an appropriate invocation of `git diff` to compare the working tree with the current commit, but restrict the comparison to `file1.txt`. Before running the command, predict how the output will differ from the previous question.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff HEAD -- file1.txt
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index e69de29..caaf2c0 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -0,0 +1,2 @@</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Staged contents of file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Unstaged contents of file1.txt</span>
</pre>

The output contains only the changes to `file1.txt`. The comparison is the same as in the previous question, but the `-- file1.txt` argument restricts the output to this file. Consequently, the changes to `file2.txt` and the deletion of `file3.txt` are not shown.

:::

<b>5. Show changes introduced in the current commit.</b>

Run the following commands to stage and commit all changes from the previous step, and make an additional commit with more changes to `file1.txt` and `file2.txt`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Add content to file1.txt and file2.txt and remove file3.txt"
$ echo "More content" >> file1.txt
$ echo "More content" >> file2.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Add more content to file1.txt and file2.txt"
</pre>

The repository now contains three commits:

<pre class="terminal">
<span class="col-hash">d42df25</span> <span class="col-yellow">(</span><span class="col-head">HEAD</span> <span class="col-yellow">-></span> <span class="col-branch-local">main</span><span class="col-yellow">)</span> Add more content to file1.txt and file2.txt
<span class="col-hash">19c0e5f</span> Add content to file1.txt and file2.txt and remove file3.txt
<span class="col-hash">55cef4f</span> Add files
</pre>

Use an appropriate invocation of `git diff` to see the changes introduced in the current commit.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff HEAD^ HEAD
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index caaf2c0..6c52455 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@</span>
 Staged contents of file1.txt
 Unstaged contents of file1.txt
<span class="col-diff-addition">+More content</span>
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file2.txt b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 5dd500d..17fce18 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/file2.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1 +1,2 @@</span>
 Unstaged contents of file2.txt
<span class="col-diff-addition">+More content</span>
</pre>

:::

<b>6. Compare two commits.</b>

Use `git diff` to compare the first commit with the third commit.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">

<span class="col-diff-addition">+Staged contents of file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Unstaged contents of file1.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+More content</span>
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/file2.txt b/file2.txt</span>

### Exercise 3 - Understanding the direction of comparisons

In this exercise, we will explore how the order of commits specified when using `git diff` affects the output. Remember that `git diff` compares two versions of a file, treating the first as the original version and the second as the modified version.

First, create a Git repository with two commits containing different versions of a file named `article.txt`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/ex03-git-diff
$ cd ~/ex03-git-diff
$ git init
$ echo "Introduction" > article.txt
$ echo "Methods" >> article.txt
$ echo "Results" >> article.txt
$ git add article.txt
$ git commit -m "Add article draft"
$ # Recreate the article draft from scratch
$ echo "Introduction" > article.txt
$ echo "Methods" >> article.txt
$ echo "Discussion" >> article.txt
$ git add article.txt
$ git commit -m "Revise article draft"
</pre>

<b>1. Compare the first commit with the second commit.</b>

Use `git diff HEAD^ HEAD` to compare the first commit with the second commit.

Before running the command, consider the following questions:

- Which commit is treated as the original version, and which is treated as the modified version?

- Which lines do you expect to be displayed as additions and deletions?

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff HEAD^ HEAD
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/article.txt b/article.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index 8353619..a5d5ce8 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/article.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/article.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@</span>
 Introduction
 Methods
<span class="col-diff-deletion">-Results</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Discussion</span>
</pre>

The first commit (`HEAD^`) is treated as the original version, while the second commit (`HEAD`) is treated as the modified version.

The line `Results` appears as a deletion because it was present in the first commit but not in the second. The line `Discussion` appears as an addition because it is present in the second commit but not in the first.

:::

<b>2. Reverse the order of the commits.</b>

Now use `git diff HEAD HEAD^` to reverse the order of the commits being compared.

Before running the command, predict how the output will differ from the previous comparison.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git diff HEAD HEAD^
<span class="col-diff-file-header">diff --git a/article.txt b/article.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-metadata">index a5d5ce8..8353619 100644</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">--- a/article.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-markers">+++ b/article.txt</span>
<span class="col-diff-hunk-header">@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@</span>
 Introduction
 Methods
<span class="col-diff-deletion">-Discussion</span>
<span class="col-diff-addition">+Results</span>
</pre>

The same two versions of the file are being compared, but their order has been reversed. The second commit (`HEAD`) is now treated as the original version, while the first commit (`HEAD^`) is treated as the modified version.

Consequently, `Discussion` is displayed as a deletion, while `Results` is displayed as an addition.

Notice that reversing the order of the commits reverses the additions and deletions, even though the contents of the two commits have not changed.

:::

<b>3. Interpreting a reverse comparison.</b>

Imagine that you have discovered a problem with the changes introduced in the second commit and are considering restoring `article.txt` to its state in the first commit.

Which of the two comparisons would be more useful for understanding the changes needed to restore the earlier version? Explain your answer.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

The reverse comparison, `git diff HEAD HEAD^`, shows the differences between the current version and the earlier version, treating the earlier version as the desired result.

In our example, it shows that restoring the earlier version would involve replacing `Discussion` with `Results`.

Remember that `git diff` only displays differences between versions of files. It does not modify files or undo commits.

:::

Wrap up by deleting the exercise repository:

<pre class="terminal">
$ cd
$ rm -rf ~/ex03-git-diff
</pre>
